I hear the weight in this question — and I want to say clearly: I don't think you're wrong to be angry about this, and I'm not going to try to smooth it over.

Here's what I found from a few Christian sources, for whatever it's worth:

**God doesn't cause it, and he doesn't excuse it.** From Cru, the Christian view is that "God is completely good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life" — and it traces suffering to sin and brokenness entering the world, not to God inflicting it ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html)).

**On human freedom and evil specifically:** EveryStudent tackles this question almost exactly as you've posed it — "why worship a God who allows horrible things, like a child being raped?" Their answer isn't a dodge so much as a hard reframe: "it is not God's fault that people choose to take the good he has created and corrupt it... We human beings are pretty much free to do as we choose." They argue that if everyone actually followed what God revealed as good, "no child would ever be raped or molested" — the harm comes from human choices, not God's design ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).

**On the "why doesn't he just stop it" question**, thelife.com pushes further into the emotional side, acknowledging that intellectual answers often aren't what a suffering child — or a suffering adult — actually needs. "A child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance." Their claim is that God's response to evil wasn't distant explanation but entering into it: in Jesus, "he has done something about evil... He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form... HE SUFFERED" ([thelife.com](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).

**And on why bad things happen even without anyone "deserving" it:** Sightline Ministry points to the account of the man born blind in John 9 — Jesus rejects the idea that suffering is always someone's fault, saying it "was not because of his sins or his parents' sins." The point there is that some suffering is tied to a world with real physical laws and real brokenness, not a targeted punishment ([Sightline Ministry](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).

I want to be honest with you: none of this makes child suffering okay, and these sources don't pretend it does. The common thread isn't "here's why it's fine" — it's "God hasn't stayed distant from this pain; he entered it in Jesus, and he promises real accountability and an end to it." Whether that's satisfying to you is a different question than whether it's a dodge — I think it's a real attempt to wrestle with something genuinely terrible.

What's underneath this for you — is there a particular situation or loss that's making this question so pressing right now?

That's a genuinely fair question — on the surface it does sound like it's saying "1=3," which would indeed be a contradiction. But Christians would say it's not actually claiming that. Here's the distinction that resolves it:

**The key move: "one" and "three" apply to different aspects of God.**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief" (https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html), the doctrine states that God is **one in essence** and **three in Person**. A contradiction would only occur if someone claimed God is three in the *same* way he is one — but that's not what's being said. So it's not "one God = three Gods," it's "one being, three persons within that one being."

Breaking that down:
- **Distinct persons**: The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are shown in Scripture to be distinct from one another — for example, the Father sends the Son into the world (John 3:16), and the Father and Son together send the Holy Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). If one sends another, they can't simply be identical to each other.
- **Each fully God**: The Bible calls the Father God (Phil. 1:2), Jesus God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit God (Acts 5:3-4).
- **Yet only one God**: Because all three share the very same essence — the same "being" — there is only one God, not three.

The German EveryStudent article "Dreieinigkeit" (https://www.duentscheidest.com/artikel/dreieinigkeit.html) puts it simply: God is present in three Persons who share the one same divine essence. It also points to that curious mixture of singular and plural language in Genesis, where God says "Let us make man in our image."

For an illustration (Cru's Spanish article and EveryStudent's English article both note illustrations have limits, but can help): water can exist as liquid, ice, or steam — different forms, same H2O. Or sunlight, heat, and radiation all coming from one sun. EveryStudent ("Can You Explain the Trinity?", https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html) frames it with a math analogy: it's not 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1 — hence the word "Tri-unity."

Honestly, as several of these sources admit, no human illustration captures it perfectly, and full comprehension isn't really possible for finite minds trying to grasp an infinite God. The claim isn't that logic is being violated, but that God's inner nature is genuinely beyond full human categorization — one being existing eternally as three distinct, relational persons who fully share that one divine nature.

Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" help clarify it, or would it be useful to look at specific Bible passages where this shows up, like at Jesus' baptism?

This is a really important and common conversation point between Muslims and Christians, so let me lay out what these sources actually say.

**The core difference**

According to Cru's article *"What Makes Christianity Different?"* (cru.org), while Muslims and Christians both revere figures like Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, "what each faith says about Jesus is radically different. In particular, Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God." The same source notes that Muslims don't believe in Jesus's crucifixion and resurrection, while these are "fundamental truths for the Christian faith."

**Why Christians see Jesus as more than a prophet**

EveryStudent's article *"Jesus in Islam"* (everystudent.com) frames it this way: Christians don't see Jesus's sonship as replacing earlier revelation but as the *fulfillment* of it — the prophets from Abraham onward pointed toward a coming figure, and Christians believe Jesus himself claimed, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

On the specific objection that calling Jesus "Son of God" sounds like blasphemy against God's oneness — a related EveryStudent article (in Slovak, *"Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely,"* everystudent.sk) explains that Christians don't understand this sonship in a physical/biological sense but a spiritual one: "Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born of a physical relationship between a man and woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit." That source also points to Isaiah's prophecy given long before Jesus's birth, calling the coming child "Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" — which Christians take as evidence this identity was anticipated, not invented later.

**On the crucifixion**

That same Slovak-language source notes that in Islam, Jesus did not actually die on the cross — the Quran (Surah An-Nisa 4:157–158) is cited as saying he was not killed or crucified, but it was only made to appear that way, and God raised him up. Christians, by contrast, hold his death and resurrection as central and historical.

---

If you're wrestling with this question personally — whether from a Muslim background, a friendship, or just genuine curiosity — I'd love to hear more about what's drawing you to it. Is there a particular piece (his identity, the crucifixion, the nature of Scripture) you'd want to dig into further?

That's a fair and honest question — and it's worth being precise about, so let me lay out exactly what's there.

**The straightforward answer: no, the Gospels never quote Jesus saying the literal English sentence "I am God."** As Sightline Ministry puts it, "the Gospels never quote Jesus saying, 'I am God,'" but they "still include statements from Jesus that clearly identify him with God" (Sightline Ministry, *Two Reasons Skeptics Believe Jesus is not God*, https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god).

Here are his actual recorded words that come closest, so you can weigh them yourself:

**John 8:58** — "Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!" According to the Jesus Film Project, Jesus is here "calling himself by the very name God used when he spoke to Moses from the burning bush (Exodus 3:14)." The reaction of the crowd (they tried to stone him) suggests they heard this as a claim to divinity (Jesus Film Project, *40 Interesting Facts about Jesus*, https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts).

**John 10:30** — "The Father and I are one." Sightline Ministry notes that a Greek scholar, A.T. Robertson, explained that the word "one" here "doesn't indicate one in person or purpose, but rather one in essence or nature" — and the hearers responded by picking up stones to kill him for it (Sightline Ministry, *Did Jesus Say He Is God?*, https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god).

**Mark 14:61-63** — At his trial, the high priest asks Jesus directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers simply, "I am." Cru points out this exchange happened when his life was on the line — he wasn't speaking in riddles here (Cru, *Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?*, https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

**John 14:9** — "Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father," also cited by Sightline Ministry as one of his clearest self-identifications with God.

So the honest picture is: Jesus never uttered the exact phrase "I am God," but he made several statements — especially "before Abraham was, I am" and "I and the Father are one" — that his own listeners understood as claims to divinity, strongly enough that they considered it blasphemy worthy of death. Whether you find those statements convincing as claims to deity is something reasonable people have wrestled with — I'd encourage you to read the passages yourself in context (John 5, 8, 10, 14, and Mark 14) and see what you make of them.

Is there a particular passage you'd like to dig into further?

   https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/10-basic-steps/1-the-christian-adventure.html
   Describes how Jesus' death "bridged the gulf between the holiness of God and the sinfulness of man," citing Colossians 1:13-14, 20-23, and notes that His resurrection completed this work (1 Corinthians 15:17).

That's a really common and fair concern, and it's worth digging into rather than just taking anyone's word for it.

Here's what the sources actually say about it:

**We don't have the original manuscripts — but we do have a huge number of copies.** According to Sightline Ministry, "we don't have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts." These copies have differences, mostly from human error in copying, but "there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (Sightline Ministry, "Has the Bible Been Altered Over the Centuries?", https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

**The numbers matter here.** Sightline Ministry's follow-up piece notes that because of "the large number of existent manuscripts," scholars "can clearly see the path of where and when mistakes and changes were made" and that "most scholars agree that the Bible has been faithfully passed down through the centuries" (Sightline Ministry, "The Bible: How Big a Deal is Human Error?", https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

**On translation specifically**, EveryStudent points out that concern about the Bible being "corrupted through translation" would be a real risk *if* translations were made from other translations — but that's not how it works. Real translations "are actually made directly from the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic" texts, based on thousands of ancient manuscripts. They cite that there are "over 24,000" handwritten manuscript copies, which "agree with each other, word for word, 99.5% of the time," and that the manuscript copies we have are dated quite close to the time of the originals (EveryStudent — Vietnamese, "Các sách của Kinh Thánh - Lịch sử của Kinh Thánh," https://www.everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html).

**Comparing ancient copies confirms this.** EveryStudent also notes we have complete Bibles dating back to around 300 A.D. that can be compared to modern Bibles and found to be "the same," and that the Dead Sea Scrolls discoveries showed the biblical text to be "highly similar, nearly 100% identical" to what we have today (EveryStudent, "Jesus in Islam," https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

**So where does that leave your uncle's claim?** It's true that we don't have the "original" physical documents, and it's true copying/translation happened many times. But the evidence suggests scholars aren't just guessing — they have thousands of manuscripts to cross-check, and the differences that exist are largely minor (spelling, word order) rather than changes that affect meaning. So the claim that "nobody can know what it originally said" doesn't match what these sources describe as the actual state of the evidence.

If you want, I'm happy to dig further into a specific piece of this — like how translators handle differences between manuscripts, or what the Dead Sea Scrolls discovery actually showed. What's prompting the question for you — is this more about trusting the Bible's content, or something else your uncle raised?

That's a really fair question — and it's one that people have wrestled with for centuries. It's not that Christians are trying to be deliberately paradoxical; there's a specific distinction being made that avoids actual contradiction.

**The key move: "one" and "three" aren't answering the same question.**

According to Cru's article *Understanding the Trinity*, the doctrine means "there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Stated differently, God is one in essence and three in person." So:

- God is **one** in *essence* (what he is — his being, his nature).
- God is **three** in *person* (who he is — distinct centers of relationship, will, and self-awareness).

A contradiction would only occur if Christians claimed God is three in the *same sense* he is one — like saying "there is one God and three gods." But that's not the claim. As the EveryStudent article *What is the Holy Trinity?* puts it, "If we were to use math, it would not be 1+1+1=3. It would be 1x1x1=1." The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit each fully possess the one divine essence — they're not three parts that add up to make God, nor three separate gods.

**Why think this at all?** Because Scripture speaks of the Father as God, the Son as God, and the Holy Spirit as God (Cru cites Philippians 1:2, Titus 2:13, and Acts 5:3-4), while also insisting there's only one God. And these three are shown to be genuinely distinct from one another — for instance, the Father sends the Son (John 3:16), and the Father and Son together send the Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33). If they were just the same person wearing different masks, that language wouldn't make sense.

**On illustrations:** Both Cru and EveryStudent offer analogies like water existing as ice, liquid, and steam, or the sun's light, heat, and radiation — but they're honest that "no illustration is going to be perfect" (EveryStudent, *What is the Holy Trinity? This Article Explains It Simply*, https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html). These are meant to loosen up our imagination, not to fully capture something about the infinite God that finite analogies can't hold.

So the honest Christian answer is: it's a **mystery**, not a **contradiction**. Mystery means it goes beyond full human comprehension; contradiction would mean it violates logic itself. Cru's article (*Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief*, https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html) makes this same point directly — the Trinity isn't a contradiction because God is one and three in *different* respects, not the same respect.

This is a really important and common question, and I want to answer it respectfully—both toward Muslim beliefs and toward what Christians actually claim.

**What Muslims believe:** As one source explains, Muslims believe Jesus is a prophet but not God in the flesh, and that Muhammad was the final prophet, sealing God's revelation after Judaism and Christianity (EveryStudent.sk, "Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely," https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame). Islam also teaches that Jesus did not actually die on the cross—that he was taken up to heaven and the crucifixion "was made to appear" that way, with some traditions holding someone else was crucified in his place (same source).

**What Christians believe, in contrast:** Cru puts it directly: "Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God... Muslims do not believe in the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, but these are fundamental truths for the Christian faith" (Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?", https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html).

**On the "Son of God" language specifically:** The EveryStudent.sk article addresses a key concern—that Islam firmly rejects the idea of God having a son as a violation of God's oneness (tawhid). It explains that Christians don't understand Jesus's sonship in a physical or biological sense, but in a spiritual sense: "Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born of a physical relationship between a man and a woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit." It points to Isaiah's prophecy, given long before Jesus's birth, calling the coming child "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (EveryStudent.sk, same article/URL as above).

That same source also raises a thoughtful point of common ground: both Islam and Christianity affirm that God has revealed himself to people in various forms—to Moses in a burning bush, to Abraham as a voice from heaven. The question it poses is: why couldn't God also take on human form to draw near to us?

**On why Christians see Jesus as more than "just a prophet":** EveryStudent's article "Jesus in Islam" (https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html) frames this as one of several respectful questions Muslims often ask, including whether it's blasphemy to call Jesus God's Son, whether Jesus really died on the cross, and why not simply view Jesus as a prophet — questions the article says it will address "with no challenges... no criticism of any religion, in any way."

If you'd like, I'm happy to dig into any one of these threads more deeply—like what Christians believe about the crucifixion, or why "Son of God" doesn't mean what it might sound like at first. What's drawing you to this question?

That's a really honest and important question — and it's a fair one to push on. Here's the direct answer: Jesus never says the literal sentence "I am God" in any Gospel. But there are places where his own recorded words make an unmistakable claim to being one with God, and these aren't paraphrases — they're quotations attributed directly to him.

The clearest one is **John 8:58**: "Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!" This is significant because "I AM" is the very name God used for himself when speaking to Moses from the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). According to the Jesus Film Project's list of facts about Jesus, this connection wasn't lost on the crowd — the Pharisees "clearly understood Jesus' claims," and John 5:18 says they wanted to kill him for it, seeing it as "making himself equal with God" (source: Jesus Film Project, https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts).

A few other direct quotations worth knowing:

- **John 10:30**: "The Father and I are one." When the crowd picked up stones to kill him for this, Jesus didn't back down — he responded, "At my Father's direction I have done many good works. For which one are you going to stone me?" (John 10:31-32), as noted by Sightline Ministry (https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god).

- **Mark 14:61-62**: On trial for his life, the high priest asks him directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers, "I am." Cru notes this exchange plainly (https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html).

- **John 14:9**: "Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father" — cited by Sightline Ministry as one of the statements that "clearly identify him with God" (https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god).

So to be precise with you: you won't find the exact phrase "I am God" on Jesus's lips. What you find are statements — in his own quoted words — that his listeners at the time understood as claims to deity, strong enough that they tried to stone him or execute him for blasphemy. Whether those statements convince you that he *is* God is a separate question from whether he *made the claim* — and based on these texts, it does appear he did, even if indirectly phrased.

Would it help to look at the context around any of these passages more closely?

I completely understand the frustration — it's smart to want to verify claims rather than just trust confident-sounding text. Here are real, linkable pages where you can read directly what Christians believe about what Jesus' death accomplished:

**1. Jesus Film Project — "Why did Jesus Have to die?"**
https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/why-jesus-had-to-die
This lays out several reasons, including that Jesus' death canceled humanity's debt: "God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having canceled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us" (quoting Colossians 2:13-14).

**2. Cru — "What Is Justification and How Does It Work?"**
https://www.cru.org/us/en/blog/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/justification.html
This explains the idea that Jesus didn't just cancel a debt but actually paid it — dying "the death we deserve" so that those who trust in him receive justification, or freedom from guilt.

**3. Cru — "Step 1: The Christian Adventure"**
https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/10-basic-steps/1-the-christian-adventure.html
This describes Jesus' death as bridging "the gulf between the holiness of God and the sinfulness of man," and notes that his resurrection is seen as completing that work — "without His resurrection and ascension, His sacrifice would have been incomplete."

**4. Cru — "Why Was Jesus Crucified?"**
https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/why-was-jesus-crucified.html
This one covers the belief that Jesus' death and the broader ministry it completed were meant to "destroy the devil's work," pointing to 1 John 3:8 and Hebrews.

**5. Jesus Film Project — "Why Is the Resurrection of Jesus So Important?"**
https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/resurrection-important
This connects Jesus' death to his resurrection, arguing that the resurrection was seen as proof that "God was fully satisfied with the sacrificial death of his Son."

A few different angles show up across these — debt paid, guilt removed, evil defeated, death overcome. They're not contradictory so much as different facets Christians use to describe the same event. If you want, I'm happy to dig into any one of these threads more deeply, or look at how different traditions emphasize them differently.

Your uncle's raising a really fair question — it's one scholars have actually studied in depth, and the short answer is: no, that concern doesn't hold up as well as it might seem at first.

**Why "copied too many times" isn't quite the issue it sounds like:**

According to Sightline Ministry, we don't have the *original* manuscripts of the Bible (called "autographs"), but we do have thousands of *copies* — and enough of them that scholars can compare them against each other to reconstruct with high confidence what the originals said. As they put it: "there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

**The numbers matter here:**

EveryStudent notes that there are nearly 25,000 hand-written manuscript copies of portions of the New Testament — a staggering number compared to other ancient texts. When historians compare these manuscripts, "the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original," with most of that remaining 0.5% being things like spelling variations that don't change meaning at all (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

**What about translation specifically?**

The concern your uncle raises — that translations made from translations could drift from the original — is a real risk in principle. But EveryVietStudent points out that reputable translations aren't made from other translations; they're made directly from the ancient Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic manuscripts (EveryVietStudent — Vietnamese, https://www.everyvietstudent.com/a/215KinhThanh.html).

**On the "human error" question:**

Sightline Ministry's related piece acknowledges that scribes did make some mistakes over the centuries, but adds: "these changes do not compromise the reliability or accuracy of the Bible we use today... scholars can clearly see the path of where and when mistakes and changes were made, because of the large number of existent manuscripts" (Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

So your uncle's instinct — that copying and translating over and over could introduce error — is reasonable to raise. But the actual manuscript evidence gives scholars real tools to check this, and it turns out the text has been preserved remarkably well. It's a great question to keep digging into rather than something to just take on faith either way — I'm glad you're asking it directly.
